name: Free Will
statement: The control over our actions that makes us morally responsible, and whether we really have it.
meaning: Free will is the significant kind of control over one's actions that agents must have in order to be morally responsible for them, to deserve praise or blame. It is standardly glossed in one or both of two ways: as the ability to do otherwise, the power to have acted differently than one did, sometimes called the leeway or alternative-possibilities conception; and as being the ultimate source or origin of one's actions, the sourcehood conception, on which the action must issue from the agent in the right way. Free will is tightly bound to moral responsibility, desert, and our practices of praise and blame. The central problem is the apparent conflict between free will and determinism, the thesis that every event, including every human choice, is necessitated by prior causes together with the laws of nature. This generates the great division of positions. Compatibilists hold that free will is compatible with determinism; incompatibilists hold that it is not. Incompatibilists split into libertarians, who hold that we do have free will and so determinism must be false, requiring some indeterminism, and free-will skeptics, sometimes called hard determinists or hard incompatibilists, who conclude that free will is an illusion. Key arguments in the debate include the consequence argument, Frankfurt cases, and Galen Strawson's basic argument, and P. F. Strawson's appeal to the reactive attitudes reframed the whole dispute.
mechanism: The free will debate is organized by how positions relate free will to determinism and to moral responsibility. If determinism is true, then given the past and the laws only one future is possible, which seems to threaten both the ability to do otherwise and the agent's status as ultimate source. Compatibilists argue the threat is illusory. Classical compatibilists, following Hobbes, Hume, and Mill, analyze free action as acting according to one's own desires without external constraint or coercion, a freedom of action that a determined agent can enjoy, and they reinterpret could have done otherwise as a conditional, would have done otherwise if one had chosen to. More recent compatibilists locate freedom in features of the agent's psychology: Harry Frankfurt in a mesh between one's effective first-order desires and one's second-order volitions, so that one acts freely when one has the will one wants, and John Martin Fischer and Mark Ravizza in guidance control exercised through a moderately reasons-responsive mechanism that is the agent's own. Incompatibilists resist. Libertarians hold we are genuinely free and so require indeterminism, spelled out either as agent-causation, in which the agent as a substance causes the action, in Chisholm and O'Connor, or as event-causal libertarianism, in Robert Kane. The consequence argument, from Peter van Inwagen, contends that if our acts are consequences of the fixed past and the laws, which are not up to us, then our acts are not up to us either. Frankfurt cases, using a counterfactual intervener, aim to show that responsibility does not require the ability to do otherwise, supporting sourcehood over leeway. Galen Strawson's basic argument urges that genuine responsibility would require being the cause of oneself, which is impossible. P. F. Strawson instead grounded responsibility in the reactive attitudes, such as resentment and gratitude, that structure human relations.

examples.text: Free will is glossed as the ability to do otherwise, and as being the ultimate source of one's action.
Classical compatibilists treat free action as doing what one wants without external constraint, compatible with determinism.
A counterfactual intervener who would have forced the same choice suggests responsibility need not require doing otherwise.

variants.name: Compatibilism versus incompatibilism
variants.text: Whether free will is compatible with determinism, dividing compatibilists from libertarians and free-will skeptics.

variants.name: The reactive attitudes
variants.text: P. F. Strawson's grounding of responsibility in attitudes like resentment and gratitude, independent of determinism's truth.

whyItMatters: Free will is one of the oldest and most consequential problems in philosophy, standing at the intersection of metaphysics, ethics, and the philosophy of mind. Its stakes are enormous, because our entire framework of moral responsibility, of desert, praise, blame, punishment, guilt, and gratitude, appears to presuppose that agents have some significant control over what they do, and the threat that determinism, or the causal order of nature more generally, might undermine that control puts these practices in question. The debate sharpens crucial distinctions, between freedom of action and freedom of the will, between the ability to do otherwise and being the source of one's actions, and between the conditions for free action and those for moral responsibility. It has generated landmark arguments, the consequence argument for incompatibilism, Frankfurt cases against the requirement of alternative possibilities, and Galen Strawson's argument that ultimate responsibility is impossible, and P. F. Strawson's influential attempt to dissolve the problem by grounding responsibility in our reactive attitudes. Contemporary work also engages the sciences, weighing what neuroscience and psychology imply about human agency. As the problem of whether and how we control our actions well enough to be responsible for them, free will is a central and enduring philosophical question.

working.text: understand it as the control needed for moral responsibility, whether as leeway or as sourcehood.
ask whether that control is compatible with every choice being necessitated by prior causes and laws.
adopt compatibilism, libertarianism, or free-will skepticism, weighing the consequence argument and Frankfurt cases.

limits: The free will problem is genuinely open, with able defenders of each major position and no consensus in sight. Compatibilism, though the majority view among philosophers, faces the charge that it changes the subject, offering only a freedom of action while leaving untouched the deeper worry that a determined agent is not the ultimate source of their will; manipulation arguments press that an agent covertly engineered to have exactly the psychology they do seems unfree even if compatibilist conditions are met. Libertarianism must explain how indeterminism could add control rather than mere randomness, the luck objection, and how agent-causation fits the natural world. Free-will skepticism must reckon with how radically it would revise our practices of blame and desert. Galen Strawson's basic argument, that true responsibility requires the impossible feat of being the cause of oneself, applies whether or not determinism is true. Some labels and details reward care: hard determinism is a traditional term that recent skeptics often replace with hard incompatibilism, sourcehood rather than aseity is the standard term, and the bearing of the Libet neuroscience experiments is much disputed. So free will robustly names the control required for responsibility, understood as a deeply contested problem where compatibilism, libertarianism, and skepticism each face serious objections.
misreadings: Free will is not merely doing what one wants; that is freedom of action, which even compatibilists distinguish from the deeper question of whether the will itself is free. Compatibilism does not claim determinism is true, only that free will would be compatible with it if it were. And the ability to do otherwise is not obviously required for responsibility, since Frankfurt cases challenge that requirement in favor of sourcehood, so treating free will as mere desire-satisfaction, compatibilism as asserting determinism, or alternative possibilities as clearly necessary, misreads the debate.
origin: The philosophical problem of the control over action required for moral responsibility, and whether it is compatible with determinism, dividing compatibilists from libertarians and free-will skeptics and shaped by the consequence argument, Frankfurt cases, and the reactive attitudes.
